newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: UNHCR to resume Kabul operations.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR to resume Kabul operations.

text.p: The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said on Wednesday it will soon resume operations in Kabul after the last of four local staff detained by the Taleban militia had been released.
The agency put most of its programmes on hold on November 21 saying it could not function without half its staff.
Apart from detaining four male staffers, the Taleban prevented seven women UNHCR staffers from working since the radical Islamic militia captured Kabul on September 27.
A UNHCR driver abducted by Taleban gunmen on October 26, in what may have been a private initiative by a local commander, was released on Tuesday, the agency said in a statement.
The other three staffers, detained as they left the UNHCR office in Kabul on November 12, were freed 10 days earlier. No charges were brought against any of the staffers.
"We're hoping that this marks a new beginning," the statement quoted Sri Wijeratne, chief of UNHCR's Afghanistan operation, as saying.

"We have now received firm assurances from the Taleban authorities that they will ensure the security of our staff in future. It is important that we all cooperate to alleviate the miserable conditions under which so many of Kabul's inhabitants are living," he said.

The UNHCR said that senior Taleban authorities had promised at a meeting with UNHCR officials in Kandahar to resolve the issue of the arrested staff and ensure the security of U.N. employees working in Taleban-controlled areas.
Two of the three staff still in custody at that time were released in Kabul three days later, it said.

The UNHCR, many of whose programmes target widows and families headed by women, said it had received encouraging indications that some of its female Afghan staff would soon be allowed to resume work. It gave no details.
The agency said that fighting in the Kabul area and the northwestern province of Badghis had displaced at least 80,000 people since September, of whom 30,000 had fled to Pakistan.
